cards.title: Expected FPT delay from small-witness decision
cards.formal: Does every self-contained \(k\)-witness problem whose decision version is fixed-parameter tractable admit an always-correct randomized enumeration algorithm with expected delay \(f(k)L^{O(1)}\), where \(L\) is the encoded input length and \(f\) is a computable function? The algorithm must output every distinct witness exactly once and terminate, with the same expected bound before the first output and after the last. This selects the expected-delay branch of the source question; deterministic delay and the weaker incremental bounds are distinct companion questions.
cards.why: Tests how far an efficient existence test can be converted into a reliably responsive generator of all small solutions. The distinction between total work and delays matters when a solution set is large and users need successive answers before enumeration finishes.
cards.status_note: Read the IPEC definitions and complete conclusion, the January 2018 author-final v4, and the publisher’s corresponding definitions and conclusion. Targeted later-work searches through 12 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of the expected-delay implication. This card explicitly selects that branch from the source’s several alternatives; it does not claim that solving it negatively settles the weaker incremental branch.

sentences: A self-contained witness is a k-element subset whose validity survives restriction to any universe containing it.
An FPT decision algorithm can therefore test whether a chosen subset contains a witness.
The selected question asks whether this always yields exact enumeration with expected FPT time between outputs, including startup and termination.
The source already controls expected total work but leaves the stronger delay guarantee open.
Incremental time, deterministic delay and enumeration with possible omissions are separate variants.

cards.definitions:
A problem instance I has an explicitly represented finite universe U and a parameter k≥1. Its witnesses form a family W(I,k) of k-element subsets of U, not a family of ordered tuples or of certificates attached to the same subset. For example, when a witness is a k-vertex set supporting a path, several paths on that same vertex set do not create several witnesses. Each output is one subset, represented by its sorted list of element indices. The output order among subsets is unrestricted. Let N=|W(I,k)|; the algorithm is not given N. Instances with k>|U| have no witnesses.

“Self-contained” means that restricting the instance to X⊆U preserves exactly the witnesses contained in X: W(I|X,k)={W∈W(I,k):W⊆X}. The restriction examines only the retained elements and their relationships, is computable in polynomial time, and has encoded length polynomial in the original length L. A decision procedure on I|X therefore answers whether X contains a witness of the original instance. This is the inclusion query INC(I,X,k). Witnesses whose validity depends on their relationships to deleted elements, such as a vertex cover of the original graph, do not automatically satisfy this property.

The premise is a deterministic algorithm deciding whether W(I,k) is nonempty in time g(k)L^a, for some computable g and constant a independent of k and I. It thus also implements inclusion queries with an FPT bound. The desired enumerator may depend on the fixed witness problem, as may f and its constant polynomial exponent, but all of them must be uniform over its instances and parameter values. This is an implication between algorithmic existence statements; it does not additionally require an effective compiler from arbitrary decision-program code, or restrict the enumerator to a black-box oracle.

For a fixed input, let τ_i be the time when the ith distinct witness has finished being written, τ₀=0, and τ_{N+1} the termination time. Expected FPT delay requires E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤f(k)(L+1)^b for every i=0,…,N, with a constant b independent of k,I,i,N. When N=0 it bounds the whole time to termination. Expectation is over the internal randomness on this fixed input, without conditioning on a particular random execution history. The algorithm never outputs a false or duplicate witness and finishes the complete list with probability one. Its bound charges all work, including any preprocessing, inclusion-query execution, duplicate handling and writing outputs. The question imposes no additional polynomial-space requirement.

An expected-incremental-FPT bound instead allows E[τ_{i+1}−τ_i]≤h(k)(L+i+1)^c, which grows with the number already output. An expected-output-FPT bound controls only the final expected time by h(k)(L+N+1)^c. Such a total bound may conceal a long wait before the next output. Dropping “expected” requires the corresponding deterministic bound. These notions are not identified with each other here. An extension query additionally asks whether some witness W satisfies Y⊆W⊆X for a prescribed Y; the premise provides no such forced-inclusion operation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated implication for all self-contained k-witness problems, or exhibit a problem satisfying its decision premise and prove that no enumerator with the stated expected-delay guarantee exists, with any complexity assumption made explicit. A bound only on final expected running time, a delay allowed to grow polynomially with the number already output, a randomized list that can omit witnesses, or a result assuming an efficient extension oracle does not settle this selected branch. The source’s deterministic and incremental companion questions require separate conclusions.

context_blocks.title: Finding one witness is not the requested enumeration guarantee
context_blocks.text: A decision algorithm applied to restricted universes provides an inclusion test. The question asks what control that information gives over the pauses while listing all distinct witness subsets.

context_blocks.title: The source proves a bound on total work
context_blocks.text: The journal Theorem 1.1 gives an always-correct randomized enumerator with expected work e^{k+o(k)}g(k)|U|^{O(1)}N when N is positive and inclusion queries take g(k)|U|^{O(1)} time. One initial inclusion test handles N=0. This is an expected-output guarantee, and the conclusion still asks about delay and incremental guarantees.

context_blocks.title: An extension oracle is extra power
context_blocks.text: The source supplies examples where efficient inclusion queries do not yield FPT extension queries unless FPT=W[1]. That obstruction to one standard route does not itself prove a lower bound against every possible enumerator.

context_blocks.title: The journal clarifies the premise
context_blocks.text: The later version formulates its broader question in terms of an FPT inclusion algorithm. For the self-contained problems retained on this card, ordinary decision supplies that operation by restriction. The paper’s approximate-enumeration results with fallible oracles have a different correctness guarantee.

cards.context:
A decision algorithm applied to restricted universes provides an inclusion test. The question asks what control that information gives over the pauses while listing all distinct witness subsets.

The journal Theorem 1.1 gives an always-correct randomized enumerator with expected work e^{k+o(k)}g(k)|U|^{O(1)}N when N is positive and inclusion queries take g(k)|U|^{O(1)} time. One initial inclusion test handles N=0. This is an expected-output guarantee, and the conclusion still asks about delay and incremental guarantees.

The source supplies examples where efficient inclusion queries do not yield FPT extension queries unless FPT=W[1]. That obstruction to one standard route does not itself prove a lower bound against every possible enumerator.

The later version formulates its broader question in terms of an FPT inclusion algorithm. For the self-contained problems retained on this card, ordinary decision supplies that operation by restriction. The paper’s approximate-enumeration results with fallible oracles have a different correctness guarantee.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
